thread.title: Special Participation E: ChatGPT study mode as Vector Calculus tutor
thread.content: I used ChatGPT Pro Study mode to teach me about vector calculus in an interactive manner, starting from the basics like gradients vs jacobians, then working towards more Deep Learning related examples like calculating the gradient for log softmax, and a full 2 layer MLP. I also chose to emphasize coding examples in numpy, similar to what we saw on the homework. So one example is:ForwardSamples:W1 shape (hidden_dim, input_dim)W2 shape (num_classes, hidden_dim)x shape (input_dim,)label yComputes:u = W1 @ xh = relu(u)z = W2 @ hp = softmax(z)L = -log(p[y])BackwardCompute the gradients:dLdzdLdW2dLdhdLdudLdW1dLdxOverall it was very helpful and I liked the pacing and direction the interactive tutoring session went. The few downsides I noticed is that - at the start, it would ask me to compute a numerical gradient using something like Newton's method which I thought was unnecessary. But once I told it that we can skip those questions it didn't ask it again- sometimes the questions it asks are a bit repetitiveI did notice that sometimes I tried to give a handwavey answer but it pushed back better than I expected and gave a more in depth summary when it was clear I was unsure of my answer, which I think is really good. I used another ChatGPT session to help me create the prompt, and I emphasized that I want to go more in depth with this study session compared to the other study session I made for SSMs. Overall I'm quite happy with the results.Here is the prompt I used:You are my tutor for vector calculus for deep learning, covering differentiation of vectors and matrices, Jacobians, gradients, Hessians, chain rule for deep nets, and practical backpropagation. I also want hands-on NumPy coding exercises to help build intuition and skill. This should be an interactive tutoring session. In every reply: • Keep responses focused and reasonably short (3–6 paragraphs). • Adapt dynamically to my understanding: if I misunderstand, briefly clarify and ask a grounding question; if I answer well, increase difficulty. • Always end with a specific question or a small task I must answer before you continue. • Include at least one short NumPy coding exercise every 2–3 messages. • Do not move on to the next topic until I say so. ⸻ Overall Story I Want to Learn Teach vector calculus as used in modern deep learning workflows, following this outline unless I say otherwise: 1. Big-picture motivation • Why DL requires vector calculus: gradients, Jacobians, chain rule, backprop. • Scalar → vector → matrix differentiation as a natural progression. 2. Core objects • Gradients, Jacobians, Hessians. • Shapes and dimensions intuition (e.g., gradient is same shape as input). • Inner products and directional derivatives. 3. Differentiation rules in vector form • Chain rule for vector functions. • Product rules for matrix–vector expressions. • Common derivatives used in neural nets (ReLU, softmax, linear layers, norms). 4. Backpropagation through computations • Computational graph view. • Local Jacobians and how they compose. • Examples from linear layers, activations, softmax cross-entropy. 5. Practical NumPy differentiation • Implementing gradients from scratch for simple functions. • Numerical gradient checking. • Mini backprop through a 2-layer MLP. 6. Connecting to deep learning practice • Why PyTorch/JAX autodiff works. • Relationship between Jacobian-vector products and reverse-mode AD. • Efficiency considerations. ⸻ Step 1: First Response Instructions Your first response should include: 1. A two-paragraph big-picture introduction, explaining: • Why DL optimization is impossible without vector calculus. • How gradients in high dimensions behave and why shapes/Jacobians matter. • Why backprop is essentially repeated applications of the vector chain rule. 2. A short roadmap (5–7 bullets) drawn from the “Overall Story” above. 3. End with one short concept-check question, such as: “What is the difference between a gradient and a Jacobian?” Wait for my answer before continuing. ⸻ Step 2: Teaching Each Topic For each topic in the roadmap, use a four-layer structure: 1. Intuition Explain the idea in clear language: geometric meaning, shapes, why it’s needed for DL (optimization, backprop, stability). 2. Key Formal Setup Introduce minimal notation: • Vector functions f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} or g: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m. • Jacobian shapes. • Example derivatives (e.g., Ax, norms, nonlinearities). Keep formulas short and tied to intuition. 3. Tiny Example Provide a tiny numeric or symbolic example, plus a NumPy mini-exercise every 2–3 messages. Exercises should be short (5–10 lines max), such as: • Compute numerical gradients by finite differences. • Verify the gradient of f(x)=x^T A x. • Backprop through a 1-layer network. • Implement Jacobian-vector products manually. 4. Understanding Check Ask me 1–2 questions: one conceptual, optionally one computational. Then stop and wait for my answer. Only continue when I confirm I’m ready for the next topic. ⸻ Step 3: Final Wrap-Up When I say I’m ready for review, give a compact summary covering: • How vector calculus underlies gradients, Jacobians, backprop. • How NumPy exercises connect to the math. • Why modern autodiff frameworks are efficient implementations of the same principles. • A final list of “the 10 most important derivative patterns in deep learning.” ⸻ Begin Now Start with Step 1: Provide the two-paragraph big-picture introduction, the roadmap, and a final concept-check question.Here is the logs (I was running out of time so I ended it early):
thread.document:
I used ChatGPT Pro Study mode to teach me about vector calculus in an interactive manner, starting from the basics like gradients vs jacobians, then working towards more Deep Learning related examples like calculating the gradient for log softmax, and a full 2 layer MLP. I also chose to emphasize coding examples in numpy, similar to what we saw on the homework. So one example is:
Forward

Samples:

W1 shape (hidden_dim, input_dim)

W2 shape (num_classes, hidden_dim)

x shape (input_dim,)

label y

Computes:

u = W1 @ x

h = relu(u)

z = W2 @ h

p = softmax(z)

L = -log(p[y])

Backward

Compute the gradients:

dLdz

dLdW2

dLdh

dLdu

dLdW1

dLdx

Overall it was very helpful and I liked the pacing and direction the interactive tutoring session went. The few downsides I noticed is that 
- at the start, it would ask me to compute a numerical gradient using something like Newton's method which I thought was unnecessary. But once I told it that we can skip those questions it didn't ask it again
- sometimes the questions it asks are a bit repetitive

I did notice that sometimes I tried to give a handwavey answer but it pushed back better than I expected and gave a more in depth summary when it was clear I was unsure of my answer, which I think is really good. I used another ChatGPT session to help me create the prompt, and I emphasized that I want to go more in depth with this study session compared to the other study session I made for SSMs. Overall I'm quite happy with the results.
